passage:
One of the oldest maxims of contract law is that a promise unsupported by consideration — some return, however small, given in exchange for the promise — is not legally enforceable. A father's casual pledge to pay his daughter's tuition, for example, would traditionally have been treated as a mere gratuitous undertaking, no more binding than a resolution to be generous. Yet courts have long recognized that this rule, if applied mechanically, produces unjust results whenever a promisee, trusting the promise, has so arranged his affairs that withdrawal of the promise leaves him materially worse off than before. Out of this discomfort grew the doctrine of promissory estoppel, which permits enforcement of a gratuitous promise where the promisor should reasonably have expected the promisee to rely on it and where such reliance has in fact occurred to the promisee's detriment.

The leading formulation in the American cases descends from a 1932 opinion of the Supreme Court of New Hampshire, which adopted what its Restatement drafters would shortly afterward call "injurious reliance" as an independent ground of liability. On this view, the promisor is held not because he has received anything in return, but because the law will not permit him to repudiate a promise whose natural and foreseeable effect was to draw the promisee into a disadvantageous course of conduct. The wrong, in short, is not a failure to perform a bargain but a kind of induced harm.

Because the doctrine cuts against the bargained-exchange tradition, courts have been cautious in applying it. Most jurisdictions require that the reliance be of a substantial and definite character, that it have been actually foreseen or readily foreseeable by the promisor, and that injustice be avoidable only by enforcement. A vague expectation of benefit, or a reliance the promisor could not have anticipated, will not suffice. Some state courts have gone further and insisted that the remedy be limited to the amount necessary to restore the promisee to the position he would have occupied absent the promise, rather than granting full expectation damages.

This last restriction is, in the present author's view, wise. Promissory estoppel was developed to prevent loss, not to confer the windfall of a completed bargain on a party who supplied no consideration. A court that awards the full value of the promise treats the promisee as though he had purchased the performance, which, by hypothesis, he has not. If the doctrine is to retain its character as a corrective to hardship rather than a substitute for the ordinary law of contract, courts should continue to measure its remedies by what was actually lost through reliance, and no more.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel is an exception to the consideration requirement whose proper scope is to remedy detrimental reliance rather than to enforce gratuitous promises in full.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The doctrine of consideration should be abandoned because it produces unjust results whenever a promisee has relied on a gratuitous promise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: American courts have been inconsistent in their application of promissory estoppel, and federal legislation is needed to bring uniformity to the area.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A 1932 decision of the Supreme Court of New Hampshire has been wrongly treated as the leading American authority on the enforcement of gratuitous promises.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts awarding full expectation damages under promissory estoppel have improperly expanded the doctrine beyond its recognized jurisdictional limits.

explanations.correct: The passage introduces the consideration rule, explains that promissory estoppel was developed to remedy its harshness where reliance has occurred, surveys the restrictions courts impose, and closes by endorsing a reliance-measured remedy. A captures both strands: the doctrine's corrective role and the limit on its remedial reach.
explanations.B: Too strong: the author does not propose abandoning consideration, only recognizing an estoppel exception where reliance is substantial.
explanations.C: Outside scope: uniformity and federal legislation are never discussed.
explanations.D: Wrong-target: the author treats the 1932 New Hampshire opinion as the leading formulation, not as wrongly so treated.
explanations.E: Too narrow: the final paragraph endorses reliance-measured remedies but does so as part of a broader thesis, not as the passage's whole point.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward limiting promissory-estoppel damages to the amount necessary to restore the promisee's pre-promise position is most accurately described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: qualified approval based on the doctrine's corrective function

choices.label: B
choices.text: reluctant acceptance on grounds of administrative convenience

choices.label: C
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement as the sole defensible rule

choices.label: D
choices.text: sharp disapproval for failing to vindicate the promisee's expectations

choices.label: E
choices.text: studied neutrality, pending further decisions from the state courts

explanations.correct: In the final paragraph the author writes that the reliance-measured limitation is 'wise' and reasons that the doctrine 'was developed to prevent loss, not to confer the windfall of a completed bargain.' That is approval, grounded in the corrective function of the doctrine — which is qualified approval, not rapture.
explanations.B: Wrong ground: the author relies on a principled argument about the doctrine's purpose, not on administrative convenience.
explanations.C: Overstated intensity: the author calls the rule 'wise,' not the sole defensible one.
explanations.D: Opposite-valence: the author affirmatively endorses the limitation.
explanations.E: Contradicts the explicit endorsement in the closing paragraph.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A traditional rule is stated, a doctrine developed to soften it is introduced and explained, restrictions on that doctrine are surveyed, and one such restriction is endorsed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two rival legal doctrines are compared, and one is shown to be superior on historical grounds.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A judicial opinion is criticized in detail, and an alternative formulation of the doctrine is proposed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An abstract principle is announced, illustrated with several hypothetical cases, and then reconciled with statutory requirements.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A legal controversy is described, the positions of each side are evaluated, and the author concludes that the question is not yet resolvable.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 states the consideration rule; paragraph 2 introduces the estoppel doctrine via the 1932 New Hampshire opinion; paragraph 3 surveys the jurisdictional restrictions; paragraph 4 endorses the reliance-measured remedy.
explanations.B: Wrong move: there are no 'two rival doctrines' being compared head-to-head; estoppel supplements consideration rather than rivalling it.
explanations.C: Wrong move: the New Hampshire opinion is cited approvingly, not criticized.
explanations.D: Wrong grain and wrong content: no sequence of hypotheticals and no reconciliation with statutes.
explanations.E: Opposite of the closing paragraph, which firmly endorses one position.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is a condition that most jurisdictions impose before enforcing a promise under the doctrine of promissory estoppel?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The promisee must have conferred some consideration, however nominal, on the promisor.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The promisor must have communicated the promise in writing to the promisee.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The promisee's reliance must have been of a substantial and definite character.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The promise must have been made in the course of a commercial transaction.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The promisee must have attempted, unsuccessfully, to bargain for the promise.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that most jurisdictions require 'that the reliance be of a substantial and definite character,' along with foreseeability and the unavoidability of injustice absent enforcement.
explanations.A: Contradicts the passage: the whole point of estoppel is that it operates where consideration is lacking.
explanations.B: No writing requirement is mentioned in the passage.
explanations.D: The passage gives a familial illustration and does not limit the doctrine to commercial settings.
explanations.E: A failed attempt to bargain is not among the conditions listed.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to a father's pledge to pay his daughter's tuition (paragraph 1) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the kind of promise that, under the traditional consideration rule, would not be enforceable

choices.label: B
choices.text: identify a category of promises to which promissory estoppel cannot properly be extended

choices.label: C
choices.text: present an example of a promise that courts have enforced under the doctrine of promissory estoppel

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast gratuitous family promises with the commercial promises discussed later in the passage

choices.label: E
choices.text: introduce a factual dispute that the remainder of the passage will undertake to resolve

explanations.correct: The example appears immediately after the statement of the consideration rule and serves to make that rule concrete: because the daughter has given nothing in exchange, the pledge is 'a mere gratuitous undertaking, no more binding than a resolution to be generous.'
explanations.B: Wrong direction: the passage does not exclude such promises from estoppel; it treats them as a setting where reliance might justify enforcement.
explanations.C: Wrong function: the example illustrates traditional non-enforceability, not a case in which enforcement has occurred.
explanations.D: No commercial/family contrast is actually drawn in the passage.
explanations.E: The example states a legal characterization, not a factual dispute.

questions.questionStem: The passage provides the most support for inferring which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A promise that induces no foreseeable change of position in the promisee is unlikely to be enforceable under promissory estoppel.

choices.label: B
choices.text: American courts have, on the whole, abandoned the requirement of consideration in ordinary contract cases.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 1932 New Hampshire opinion has been formally overruled in most jurisdictions that once followed it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A promisee who has suffered no material harm may still recover full expectation damages where the promisor's conduct is egregious.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promissory estoppel is best understood as a specialized extension of the law of fraud.

explanations.correct: The author emphasizes that the reliance must be substantial, foreseeable, and detrimental. A promise that induces no foreseeable change of position fails both the foreseeability and the detriment conditions, so enforcement under estoppel would be unlikely.
explanations.B: Too-strong: the passage says only that estoppel is an exception, not that consideration has been abandoned generally.
explanations.C: Outside scope: the status of the 1932 opinion as 'leading' suggests the opposite.
explanations.D: Contradicts the author's endorsement of reliance-measured remedies.
explanations.E: Outside scope: the passage characterizes estoppel as a response to induced harm, not as an extension of fraud law.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's position that promissory-estoppel remedies ought to be limited to the amount necessary to restore the promisee's pre-promise position?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Historical surveys of the doctrine show that early American courts granted full expectation damages only where a bargained-for exchange was present.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several state legislatures have recently codified the consideration requirement without mentioning promissory estoppel.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Commentators have praised the 1932 New Hampshire opinion for its clarity of language.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Juries tend to calculate expectation damages more easily than reliance damages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many gratuitous promises are made informally and not reduced to writing.

explanations.correct: The author's position is that expectation damages are reserved for promises supported by consideration, while estoppel should remedy only loss from reliance. A historical finding that early courts granted expectation damages only where a bargain was present directly supports that allocation of remedies.
explanations.B: Neutral: legislative silence on estoppel does not bear on the measure of its remedies.
explanations.C: Off-target: praise for the opinion's clarity says nothing about the proper measure of damages.
explanations.D: Actually cuts the other way: ease of calculation would be a reason to award expectation damages, not to confine recovery to reliance.
explanations.E: Outside scope: writings and formality are not the issue; the measure of recovery is.

passage:
When a federal agency issues a regulation interpreting the statute it is charged with administering, the courts must decide how much weight to give that interpretation in subsequent litigation. For several decades, American reviewing courts followed a two-step approach articulated by the United States Supreme Court in a 1984 case involving the Environmental Protection Agency. Under that approach, a court first asks whether the statute is clear on the precise question at issue; if it is, the court enforces the plain meaning and the agency's view is beside the point. If instead the statute is genuinely ambiguous, the court proceeds to the second step and defers to the agency's interpretation so long as the interpretation is reasonable — even if the court, writing on a blank slate, would have read the statute differently.

The justification most commonly offered for this deference is that Congress, in leaving a statute ambiguous, has implicitly entrusted the gap-filling task to the expert agency rather than to the generalist judiciary. Agencies, after all, possess technical knowledge and continuing engagement with the regulated community that courts cannot readily match. A second justification rests on political accountability: because the agency is ultimately answerable to the elected executive, interpretive choices with policy consequences are thought to be better left with an accountable actor than with appointed judges.

These justifications have, however, invited objection. Critics note that a court asked whether a statute is 'clear' is exercising precisely the interpretive judgment the doctrine later disclaims; the result is a framework in which difficult questions of statutory meaning are partly resolved by a prior determination that the question itself is hard. Moreover, expertise and accountability explain why an agency might be a good source of policy, but they do not obviously explain why a court should depart from its ordinary duty to say what the law is.

The force of these criticisms varies with the type of statute at issue. Where a provision is highly technical — a tariff schedule, an emissions standard, an actuarial formula — the expertise rationale retains most of its persuasive power, and judicial deference can be justified on grounds that are genuinely institutional rather than merely traditional. Where, however, the disputed provision concerns the scope of the agency's own authority, deference is harder to defend: one does not ordinarily permit a party to interpret the document that defines its own powers. Reviewing courts would do well, in this author's view, to preserve deference in the first setting while withholding it in the second. Such a division respects the expertise that originally justified the doctrine without extending it to the very questions on which a disinterested judgment is most needed.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Judicial deference to agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes is justified when the disputed question is technical but not when it concerns the scope of the agency's own authority.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The two-step framework announced in 1984 should be abandoned because its first step already requires the interpretive judgment the second step disclaims.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Federal agencies, being politically accountable through the executive, are better positioned than courts to resolve all genuinely ambiguous statutory questions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The expertise and accountability rationales for judicial deference have proved insufficient and should be replaced by a new rationale grounded in constitutional structure.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts reviewing agency interpretations tend to overestimate the degree of ambiguity in the statutes they are asked to apply.

explanations.correct: The passage presents the two-step deference framework, summarizes the expertise and accountability justifications, reports criticisms of those justifications, and culminates in the author's recommended division: defer on technical provisions, withhold deference on questions about the agency's own authority.
explanations.B: Too-strong: the author records the critical point but does not call for abandoning the framework; he proposes a principled division instead.
explanations.C: Contradicts the closing paragraph, which denies deference in a key category of cases.
explanations.D: The passage does not propose a new constitutional rationale; it argues for domain-sensitive application of the existing ones.
explanations.E: Outside scope: overestimation of ambiguity is not discussed.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A doctrine is described, the common justifications for it are presented, objections are reported, and a qualified prescription is offered.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A historical controversy is surveyed and resolved in favor of one of two long-standing positions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A judicial opinion is praised, its critics are rebutted, and the opinion is reaffirmed without qualification.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several competing doctrines are set out, and their relative merits are ranked according to a single criterion.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A statutory scheme is described, and the author argues that Congress should amend it.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 sets out the two-step doctrine; paragraph 2 gives the expertise and accountability justifications; paragraph 3 records objections; paragraph 4 offers the author's division-based prescription.
explanations.B: Wrong move: no historical controversy between two parties is set up and resolved.
explanations.C: Wrong move: the opinion's framework is critiqued, not reaffirmed without qualification.
explanations.D: Wrong move: only one doctrine is in view; there is no ranking.
explanations.E: Wrong target: the author addresses courts, not Congress, and proposes no statutory amendment.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is a justification commonly offered for deferring to an agency's interpretation of an ambiguous statute?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Agencies, having been created by the legislature, speak with its delegated authority on all statutory questions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The agency is answerable to the elected executive and is therefore politically accountable for interpretive choices with policy consequences.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Judicial review of agency action is constitutionally disfavored in the administrative context.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reviewing courts lack the authority to declare any federal statute ambiguous.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Agencies tend to adopt interpretations that favor regulated parties, which courts are then free to accept.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states the accountability rationale almost verbatim: 'the agency is ultimately answerable to the elected executive,' so interpretive choices with policy consequences 'are thought to be better left with an accountable actor than with appointed judges.'
explanations.A: Overstated: the passage does not claim agencies speak with delegated authority on all questions.
explanations.C: Contradicts the passage, which describes active judicial review.
explanations.D: Contradicts step one of the framework, which authorizes courts to determine whether a statute is clear.
explanations.E: Outside scope: agency bias toward regulated parties is not discussed.

questions.questionStem: It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Institutional competence is a more defensible basis for deference in cases involving technical regulatory details than in cases about the boundaries of agency power.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A statute should be treated as unambiguous whenever the reviewing court finds the agency's interpretation unpersuasive.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deference to agency interpretations is inappropriate whenever the statute at issue has significant policy consequences.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The expertise rationale for deference is generally stronger than the accountability rationale.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Federal courts should defer to agency interpretations only when both parties to the litigation request such deference.

explanations.correct: The closing paragraph distinguishes two settings and endorses deference in the technical one while withdrawing it where the agency is, in effect, interpreting the scope of its own power. That is precisely the institutional-competence distinction captured in A.
explanations.B: Overreach: the author nowhere suggests that persuasiveness of the interpretation determines ambiguity.
explanations.C: Too-strong and not supported: the author distinguishes types of ambiguity, not the presence of policy consequences.
explanations.D: Not claimed: the passage does not rank the two rationales generally.
explanations.E: Outside scope: party preferences are not mentioned.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to 'a tariff schedule, an emissions standard, an actuarial formula' (paragraph 4) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: identify kinds of statutory provisions for which the expertise rationale retains substantial force

choices.label: B
choices.text: show that most federal regulatory provisions are too technical for any court to evaluate

choices.label: C
choices.text: catalogue examples of provisions that have been found to be clear at step one of the framework

choices.label: D
choices.text: illustrate the kinds of statutes most likely to exceed the agency's granted authority

choices.label: E
choices.text: contrast modern regulatory statutes with earlier, less specialized forms of legislation

explanations.correct: Immediately before the list the author writes that 'where a provision is highly technical,' the expertise rationale retains most of its persuasive power. The enumeration provides concrete illustrations of 'highly technical' provisions for which deference is appropriate.
explanations.B: Overstated: the author does not claim courts cannot evaluate such provisions, only that deference there is justified.
explanations.C: Wrong target: step one concerns clarity, not technicality; the provisions listed are not being characterized as clear.
explanations.D: Opposite of the function: these examples illustrate deference-appropriate cases, not authority-exceeding ones.
explanations.E: No historical contrast with earlier legislation is drawn in the passage.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the critics described in paragraph 3 is most accurately characterized as

choices.label: A
choices.text: partial agreement, treating their objections as sound in some settings but not others

choices.label: B
choices.text: unqualified endorsement, accepting every point they raise

choices.label: C
choices.text: dismissive rejection on the ground that the critics misunderstand the doctrine

choices.label: D
choices.text: detached neutrality, refusing to take any position on the critics' arguments

choices.label: E
choices.text: mild exasperation at critics who have offered the same objections for decades

explanations.correct: In the final paragraph the author writes that 'the force of these criticisms varies with the type of statute at issue,' then accepts the critics' point for scope-of-authority questions while rejecting it for technical ones. That is partial agreement.
explanations.B: Too-strong: the author retains deference for technical cases, contrary to the critics' broader challenge.
explanations.C: Opposite-valence: the critics' objections are treated as at least partly correct.
explanations.D: Contradicted by the author's explicit prescription.
explanations.E: No exasperation or historical frustration is expressed.

questions.questionStem: The author's proposed division is most clearly exemplified by which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A reviewing court defers to an agency's technical calculation of permissible pollutant concentrations under an ambiguous emissions statute, but declines to defer to the agency's determination that the statute authorizes it to regulate a new category of pollutant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A reviewing court defers to an agency's interpretation of a statute regardless of whether the statute is ambiguous, reasoning that agencies are politically accountable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A reviewing court rejects an agency's interpretation of an ambiguous statute because the court believes its own reading is superior on the merits.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A reviewing court refuses to decide a statutory question, remanding the entire case to the agency for further factfinding.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A reviewing court defers to an agency's claim to have acquired authority to regulate a new industry, while reviewing the agency's technical rules de novo.

explanations.correct: The author's proposal is to preserve deference where the provision is technical and withhold it where the dispute concerns the scope of the agency's own authority. A instantiates precisely that division: deference on pollutant concentrations (technical), no deference on whether the statute authorizes regulation of a new category (scope of authority).
explanations.B: Ignores step one of the framework and the author's selective approach; deference is unconditional here.
explanations.C: Does not track the author's distinction; it rejects deference on the merits rather than on the technical/scope division.
explanations.D: A procedural remand is unrelated to the deference question the author addresses.
explanations.E: Inverts the author's division, deferring on scope while reviewing technical matters de novo.
